However, magnetic experiments appear less clearly because the forces are weaker in round iron tools. The variety of declinations is shown by iron needles <note>original: "obelis ferreis"</note> at various latitudes of the <term>terrella</term> <gloss>a spherical lodestone representing the Earth</gloss>.

<note>A circular diagram represents a <term>terrella</term>. An outer circle is labeled "Circle of Virtue" </note><note>original: "Orbis Virtutis"</note>. Inside, a shaded sphere representing the <term>terrella</term> has a horizontal "Axis" drawn through it. Along the circumference of this inner sphere, several small iron needles are depicted at various latitudes. At the equatorial points, the needles lie flat against the surface. As they move toward the top and bottom poles, they incline at increasingly steep angles, until they stand perfectly vertical at the magnetic poles.

The declination of magnetic iron over the <term>terrella</term> is shown by various equal iron wires, the length of a barleycorn, arranged over the meridian. The wires at the equator are directed by the power of the stone toward the poles, and they lie down upon the body in the plane of its horizon. The closer they are placed to the poles, the more they are raised by their convertible nature. At the poles themselves, they tend perpendicularly toward the very center. But iron needles do not stand upright correctly unless they are on a vigorous stone, if they are longer than they should be.

### C H A P. III.

### A demonstrative instrument, indicating by the power of the stone the degrees of declination from the horizon of each latitude.

<summary>This page explains how magnetic inclination (dip) changes relative to a spherical magnet, demonstrating that iron needles align with the magnetic field at various latitudes until they stand vertically at the poles.</summary>
